newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - Feb 28.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - Feb 28.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories on Friday:

* The U.S. Internal Revenue Service on Thursday banned a popular type of corporate financing technique on Wall Street known as "fast pay" or "step down" preferred stock, effectively halting billions of dollars of transactions.

* Financier Carl Icahn sold his 7.3 percent stake in RJR Nabisco Holding, making an estimated profit of at least $100 million and ending his 17-month proxy battle to force the company to spin-off its food business.

* Hong Kong's Dickson Concepts International Ltd is preparing an offer to acquire Barney's in a deal which some say values the New York-based retailer for less than the $350 million bid Dickson had been expected to make.

* In an example of how statistics can be misleading, each of three funds managed by mutual-fund whiz Garrett Van Wagoner beat stock market averages last year, yet Van Wagoneer lost roughly $1 out of every $10 entrusted to him by investors.
* Mutual funds took in net new cash of $29.4 billion in January, but investors are moving to relatively more conservative stock funds.
* The Dow industrials fell 58.11 points to 6,925.07 in heavy trading of technology stocks. The Nasdaq 100 index lost 32.25 points to 848.49, the biggest one-day drop since July 23.
* 3Com shares fell $4 to $35 and those of U.S. Robotics fell $1.875 to $59.125 a day after 3Com proposed a $7.3 billion acquisition of U.S. Robotics.
* New York law firm Milbank, Tweed, Hadley & McCloy has been accused in court motions of conflicts of interest in a Federal bankruptcy filing involving mining company Bucyrus Erie.
* Orders for durable goods ordered rebounded in January to a larger-than-expected 3.6 percent rise, increasing the possiblity of an interest rate hike by the Federal Reserve.
* In Wall Street's first compensation disclosure for the season, Morgan Stanley said three of its top officers earned more than $10 million each last year.
* Dallas-based Triton Energy agreed to pay $300,000 to settle charges from the Securities and Exchange Commission that a subsidiary paid bribes to Indonesian government officials.
* Broadcast industry executives defended the current system of rating television programs in testimony before the U.S. Senate.
* American Express vice president Kenneth Chenault was appointed the company's president and number two executive.

* Isis Pharmaceuticals said its treatment for an inflammatory bowel condition showed promising results in a Phase II study, the first evidence of therapeutic benefit with a systematically administered antisense drug.
* Fujitsu Ltd said it would open a $122 million research and development centre in New York's Rockland County.
